doc.title: Jean Bach interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995

title: Ellington's opera line and stories at the Ottawa Ellington Society
summary: His robe-clad welcome, the opera he promised everyone, and her jive-turkey stories that the Ellington society disliked.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: That’s it. So Ellington finally came in, in a stunning silk robe, and very courtly, “how lovely to see you.” I said, “well you did say to come by.” I looked like, well I can’t say co-ed, ‘cause we only had girls and boys schools then, but you know I had the little bowler hat and the polo coat and the little white gloves and everything. And so years later, Bob Bach, my late husband, was doing a special on Ellington for PBS. And he got what they call sort of “witness spots” you know for people that had known him, and told little highlights about their lives. And of course I had nine million adventures, I couldn’t wait to get on. But how they did it was there was this director kneeling, sort of our of camera range, asking questions. And he asked me the oddest questions. And one he asked me was had Ellington ever mentioned an opera to me. Now it turns out that, that was a line he used with everybody you know. He’d meet you and he’d say, “you are so right for a part in my opera,” he said. “It has to be an intelligent handsome man with great poise and I can just see you in this role, and I don’t know whether you’d be uncomfortable singing, it doesn’t have to be a singing role.” He would lay it on with a trowell. And I mean dogs and cats, women, children, men, anybody, he didn’t care. A friend of mine, Casper Reardon, the jazz harpist, he told him he had a part, you know he was to write a part in for a harpist. So I guess they thought they’d get some juicy story from me. So I said, “yes, that first day that I went to see him he told me all about this opera he was working on, but no he didn’t say he was going to put me in the opera” he said, “Marian Anderson.” But you see how smart he was? That would impress a little college girl more. “Marian Anderson’s going to be in an opera.”
He was never at a loss, was he?

Oh, please. I had a list of, I did a little talk about this, up in Ottawa at the, there’s an International Ellington Society that meets every year in a different country. And a few years ago it was up in Ottawa. And they knew that I’d known him forever. And they said “do you want to just talk about the personal side?”— because I don’t claim to be a great musicologist. I said, “sure, because I’ve got a bundle of stories.” And I’m telling these stories about what a jive turkey he was you know. How he’d put you on. And those people didn’t think it was too funny. Because see he’s sacred. It’s like, they’re like Moonies. And I mean the fingernail clippings and the —
They didn’t want to hear that side of him. © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -6-
No, no. It didn’t go over too well. But I had a lot of funny stories.
